meanings.note: Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).
Friendly collective address for coworkers in a room or message.
Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Visual chart of numbers on a slide or report.

examples.text: Isso aqui é um gráfico, né?

meanings.note: Ubiquitous spoken contraction of não é used to invite agreement.

examples.text: Isso aqui é um gráfico, né?
examples.trans: This here is a chart, right?

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Plural addressee pronoun across Brazil, taking third-person plural verb forms.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you all look closely, there are numbers.
Are you all going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Used as a quick imperative olha! (look!) and in future subjunctive se vocês olharem (if you look).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Modifies a verb to mean well or carefully, as in olhar bem (look closely).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Indefinite determiner or pronoun; plural alguns means some or a few.

examples.text: Alguns são bons, outros são ruins.
examples.trans: Some are good, others are bad.

meanings.note: Numeric figure in data or counting.
Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
Everyday Brazilian word for bad; plural spells the nasal ending as ruins.

examples.text: Alguns são bons, outros são ruins.
examples.trans: Some are good, others are bad.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Gerund vendo pairs with estar (tá vendo, do you see), and tem que ver means we have to look into it.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
We need to look into that later.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Vamos seguir moves a meeting along to the next topic or slide.

examples.trans: We have to look into it. Let's move on.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Between article and noun (a mesma coisa) it means the same.

examples.trans: We work on the same team.

meanings.note: Very frequent general noun; singular muita coisa naturally translates as a lot of things.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: English office loanword pronounced with an initial [is-] and final [-dʒi] in Brazil.

examples.trans: Let's go to the next slide.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
Used standalone in Brazilian speech as the everyday informal sorry.

examples.trans: I want you to go in too.

meanings.note: Time between midday and evening; boa tarde! greets or bids farewell in the afternoon.
